A critical role for the PM is to identify, track and monitor risks to minimize impacts to projects. Responsibilities include timely resolution with clear accountability and date due, escalation as appropriate, early identification of risks, and tracking and monitoring dependencies.

Establishing a project risk management process


A critical role for the PM is to manage risks and minimize their impacts to the project. Responsibilities include upfront, proactive identification of risks, identification of risk management strategies and contingent actions, and tracking and monitoring of risks on an ongoing basis.

Risk overview

Risks are potential events that have a negative effect on the project success. Risk has many dimensions including strategic, operational, regulatory, reputational, technical, and others.

A project risk is a characteristic of a specific project, a circumstance of the project, or a feature of the project environment that is recognized to have a potentially adverse effect on the project or the quality of its deliverables. Risks are inherent in any project. They cannot be eliminated entirely, but many of them can be anticipated and subsequently reduced. Due to the dynamic nature of the project, risks will change. Thus, risk identification is an iterative process that continues throughout the project life cycle.

Risk examples include the following:

  • Scope – the work product definitions are unclear, which could lead to difficulty when reporting progress or gaining final acceptance by the client
  • Timeline – there are a significant number of dependencies between the project workstreams. A delay in one may cause cascading delay in several others
  • Economics – client delays or other inefficiencies in performing the required work create budget overruns and affect profitability
  • Resources – key client or EY personnel may be unavailable due to scheduling conflicts
  • Communications – client will not finance communication activities recommended for managing stakeholders during the project.

In some cases, the risks may not directly relate to the scope of work that EY is performing, but could relate to other matters that can impact the project. For example, a third party is responsible for the implementation of an enterprise resource planning system. Even though EY plays an advisory role, both the client and EY should be interested in risks faced by the third party element of the project.

Identifying, assessing and managing risk

The objective of risk identification is finding risks directly relevant to the project, not creating an exhaustive listing of unlikely events. Of the risks identified, the PM selects those that directly relate to the critical success factors of the project and to specific work streams or activities within the project. As each risk is identified, risk management mitigation strategies and contingent actions should be developed with the objective of lowering the overall risk of the project and its impact if it is actually manifested.

A risk mitigation strategy lowers the probability that an identified risk factor will occur. A contingent action is a pre-planned response to reduce the impact of a risk when it occurs. For example, if there is concern that the client will not agree to the content of a report, a typical mitigation approach is to include time devoted to reviewing a draft report and reconciling differences.

The more complex or risky the project, the more it is necessary that a formal risk management process is followed to identify, prioritize, track, and manage risks. A formal method of risk management is especially necessary when:

  • There are a large number of risks that collectively could have high impact
  • The risk management approach adds cost (e.g., if contingency planning or risk mitigation activities are required)
  • The risks adversely affect the timeline (e.g., if the timeline is extended to reduce risk)
  • The risks adds to/subtracts from the planned work of EY or the client (e.g., work shifts from one party to the other as a form of mitigation)

Understanding the risk environment includes identifying the dependencies between the desired outcome (e.g., the work product(s) and results of the project) and the potential events that could have a negative effect. Considerations include:

  • External dependencies — changes in laws or regulations, third party involvement
  • Organizational risks — lack of stakeholder buy-in, merger/acquisition
  • Planning risks — uncertainty in scope, timeline, economics
  • Scope risk — unclear definition of in/out of scope
  • Schedule risk — uncertainty in timeline, complex interdependencies
  • Resource risk — lack of availability, competency
  • Benefits risks — insufficient data upon which to base assumptions for the business case
  • Change risks — organizational commitment may not be sufficient
  • Technical risks — technology may not perform as expected
  • Performance risk — unrealistic performance requirements/expectations

Each identified risk should be assessed using two dimensions:

  1. Risk Probability
  2. Risk Impact

Risk Probability

Risk Probability is a measure of the likelihood that a certain risk will occur and negatively affect the project (i.e., probability of occurrence). The probability of occurrence for the risk element should be defined on a level from 1-5. (refer table below - “Calculating Risk Factor”).

Risk Impact

Risk Impact is a measure of the anticipated degree of impact that the risk, if it occurs, will have on the project. The degree of impact related to the risk element is calculated based on three inputs – Technology, Schedule and Cost on a level from 1-5.

Risk Factor

The Risk Factor is calculated as the combination (multiplication) of the probability and the highest impact. For example:

If Risk Probability = 3
If Risk Impact – Technology = 3
If Risk Impact – Schedule = 4
If Risk Impact – Cost = 1
Then the Risk Factor = Risk Probability * Risk Impact = 3 * 4 = 12

Developing the Risk Management Approach

When developing the overall risk management approach, the (PM) need to consider alternatives such as risk mitigation strategy, contingency planning, altering scope to avoid risk, or transferring the responsibility for an activity to distribute the risk among the project participants (i.e., a task EY considers too risky could be assigned to the client or a third party instead).

The mitigation plan is an “actionable” plan that can be effectively translated into formal action items and to which ownership for execution can be assigned. The mitigation strategy is executed throughout the project’s lifecycle to limit the impact of the risk on the project.

Contingency plans, by their very nature are triggered once the risk occurs. PMs should continually monitor project risks to determine contingency plans and activate as warranted. Activating a contingency plan may require re-planning or changes in the overall project approach such as:

  • Scope changes (add or remove)
  • Adding quality activities to the project scope/schedule to mitigate risk
  • Contingency planning (proactively defining an alternative course of action prior to a risk event)
  • Changing the resource plan (e.g. Using more experienced resources to perform difficult or risky tasks)
  • Altering roles and responsibilities

Even after aligning the quality and risk management approaches, it is likely that risks will remain (i.e., for some risks there may not be a feasible quality activity that sufficiently controls the risk). This drives the need for applying risk management strategies such as:

  • Avoidance — Add or reduce scope to avoid risky elements
  • Transference — Assign responsibility for risk to the client or another party
  • Mitigation — Perform additional work (e.g., Quality reviews) to reduce probability
  • Acceptance — Acknowledge the event may occur, but plan optimistically

During the Execute phase, the risk management approach described above should be used. As risks are identified, they should be evaluated and communicated to the appropriate parties. The PM needs to work with the client to agree to a similar process. The objectives are:

  • Identify relevant risks
  • Perform timely analysis of the risks
  • Communicate status of new or existing risks (especially changes in status)
  • Make risk management decisions on a timely basis; escalate as needed
  • Track the results of risk management activities and make adjustments as needed
  • Actively manage risks that occur in the issue management process

Underpinning the entire risk management process are key risk management principles, including:

  • Risks to be identified and assessed at outset – to include in business case
  • Organizational culture to encourage people to raise risks, not hide them
  • Organization’s risk appetite is communicated and understood
  • Risk awareness not risk aversion is what’s needed
  • Risk management process is signed off by suitably senior client personnel
  • Risks are ‘owned’ by the person closest to them
  • Effort to be focused on mitigating high priority (high risk factor) risks
  • Mitigate collective areas of risk
  • Risks’ status to be reviewed regularly
  • Risks to be reported at key governance forums, to escalate actions and aid decision-making
